PAGE: Performance (https://httpjet.net/docs/performance)
SUMMARY: Measured throughput by regime: loopback three-way benchmarks, the origin cache result, production attribution, sendfile and kTLS receipts, and PGO discipline.
==============================================================================

# Performance

httpjet is fast — and these docs are strict about *where* the time goes. Every figure names its regime, because a **loopback benchmark** (synthetic, on-box, PGO build) is not the same thing as **production telemetry** (real CDN-fronted traffic). The short version: on a Cloudflare-fronted PHP site, almost all wall time is PHP, and httpjet's own CPU is a rounding error.

        ~908 k rps   h2 static, c=50, dedicated-host loopback
        44.8 k rps   PHP/LSAPI over HTTP/1.1, PGO loopback
        101 ×   cache hit vs the same page through PHP
        0.2 %   httpjet's share of production request latency
        1.55 IPC   h2 hit path at saturation (hardware counters)
        0.0002 flt   v0.1.5 h2 static minor page faults/req

## Read the regime, not just the number

           loopback benchmark · synthetic, on-box, PGO
           production telemetry · real CF-fronted traffic
           hardware counters · perf at saturation

A loopback benchmark removes the network, real TLS handshakes and the CDN — it isolates the server's code path, which is exactly what you want to compare two servers and exactly what you must not generalize to end-user latency. Production telemetry measures what users feel, dominated by the backend and the edge. The same server shows ~908k req/s on loopback and ~0.2% of user-visible latency in production; those answer different questions.

## Performance across builds — interactive presentation

Every benchmark campaign from the initial Phase 1–7 baseline (`0.0.1`, June 2026) through the October 2026 zero-fault pooling release (`v0.1.5`) is recorded below with its exact regime, commit, and CSV receipt. Use the **All-Builds Curve vs LiteSpeed & nginx** below to see the full trajectory on one canvas, or step through the **13 build slides**, **Workload Trajectories**, and **Build-vs-Build Diff**.

## Loopback throughput

The primary dataset is the August 2026 **dedicated-host three-way** (httpjet vs OpenLiteSpeed vs nginx on a quiet box, all release/PGO-equivalent builds). The June PGO campaign against a commercial-LiteSpeed baseline remains the PHP-path reference.

> [Benchmark Chart: h2-static — HTTP/2 static throughput by concurrency (dedicated-host loopback · 2026-08-27 · empty bodies · req/s)]

One h2 connection is not a ceiling (~58k req/s at c=1), and throughput keeps rising with concurrency instead of collapsing; the earlier "h2 collapses past c=50" shape belonged to the June build and its measurement conditions, not the transport. HTTP/1.1 empty bodies at c=1000: ~202k vs OpenLiteSpeed's ~183k.

> [Benchmark Chart: heavy-rewrite — Heavy .htaccess static (806-line chain, /robots.txt) (PGO three-way · 2026-08-28 · c=100 · req/s)]

> [Benchmark Chart: memo-ab — Fast-path memo, same binary A/B (forum chain · /robots.txt · c=100 · req/s)]

> [Benchmark Chart: php-h1 — PHP over LSAPI, HTTP/1.1 (loopback · PGO build · 2026-06 · req/s)]

## The origin cache result

The single largest performance fact about the real workload is not a micro-optimization — it is the origin page cache . For the cacheable fraction of traffic, a hit replaces an entire PHP render with a memory (or tmpfs) copy.

> [Benchmark Chart: cache-vs-php — One forum page: cache hit vs full PHP render (HTTPS loopback · PGO · 152 KB page · req/s)]

A 2026-08-30 refresh under shared-box conditions (live production on the same host — directional only) put cache-hit serves at ~5.4k req/s h2 and ~6.7k h1 on real `/help/*` pages. The production hit ratio reads low for a structural reason: ~51% of origin GET-200s are one-shot bot crawls whose repeat interval exceeds any TTL, so no origin tier can absorb them — the lever there is edge TTL.

## Where the time actually goes

> [Benchmark Chart: attribution — Where a production request spends its time (live sample · 2026-08-30 · mean request 9.99 ms)]

        ⎁   Measured
Across millions of production requests, the `lsphp` render is **86.5–98.8% of request wall time**. httpjet's own CPU is about **0.2%** — roughly **138 µs per request**, ~38 µs per cache hit, and that includes TLS, HTTP/2, rewrite, cache lookup and access logging. The 2026-08-30 sample: mean request 9.99 ms, 8.96 ms of it LSAPI TTFB, rewrite 5.4 µs, cache lookup 3.2 µs; pool acquire p99.9  production telemetry · --telemetry-file + --php-slow-log

If httpjet is 0.2% of latency, halving its CPU shaves ~0.1% off a page — imperceptible. Turning a PHP render into a cache hit removes the other ~99%. That asymmetry is why the project stopped shaving the serving path and invested in the cache, PHP/opcache tuning and raising the cacheable fraction.

## At the instruction floor

        ⎁   Measured
At saturation the h2 cache-hit path shows **IPC 1.55**, a **0.31% branch-miss rate** and **1.6 L1d misses per 100 instructions**: execution is efficient and the bottleneck is instructions retired per request, not locality. Futex traffic (~85% of syscall time) turned out to be idle parking and cross-thread waker churn — the box was ~50% idle at the apparent ceiling — not lock contention.
 perf stat / strace · off-CPU analysis

Two structural moves followed: the global **mimalloc** allocator (fewer arena futexes across the per-core monoio workers plus the tokio side-runtime) and the **on-core fast path** with the finished-response memo, which removes pipeline work rather than speeding it up. The October 2026 campaign (`0.0.9`–`0.1.5`) extended this to the remaining hot paths: keeping static-missing 404s and non-cacheable PHP GETs off the fast-path double lookup (−14.5% CPU on cookied guest pages), memoizing per-file `.htaccess` access rule matches (`access_decision_for_request` 13% → 2.7% of process CPU), extending the certified-peer idle window via `--trusted-proxy-idle-secs 1800` (cutting full TLS handshakes per request by 28% on x86 and 78% on ARM), tuning per-vhost dictionary zstd levels via `--page-cache-dict-level` (cutting ARM dictionary encode from ~50% to 11% of tokio CPU), and pooling transient response/TLS buffers and h2/bridge task slots (`hj_core::recycle::BODY_BUFS`) so sparse size classes do not page-fault under `MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY=0`.

## File egress: sendfile and kTLS

> [Benchmark Chart: sendfile — File egress receipts (1 MiB bodies, c=50) (loopback · 2026-09-09 · req/s)]

Plain-TCP H1 file bodies leave through bounded nonblocking `sendfile(2)`; TLS 1.3 H1 can too under kernel TLS, but only when `--ktls=auto` finds a physical NIC with active `tls-hw-tx-offload`. The production host's virtual NIC reports `off [fixed]`, and forcing software kTLS there measured slightly *worse* — which is exactly why `auto` refuses it. Details: Protocol stacks .

## The codegen tier — PGO + mimalloc

Production binaries combine profile-guided optimization, the mimalloc allocator and `-C target-cpu=native`. The checked-in `scripts/build-pgo.sh` is the classic three-step — instrument, drive a representative loopback workload (h2 cache hits dominant, plus h2/h1 static and PHP), merge and rebuild — with frame pointers kept so the pprof endpoint can symbolize the live binary. Its workload and CPU tuning belong to one deployment; build a neutral release artifact separately.

        !   A non-PGO benchmark is not a benchmark
Debug builds are ~5× slower and meaningless. Even a plain release build differs from PGO by enough (~10% from binary layout alone) to fake a regression: build both sides the same way and interleave runs. The bench harness (`scripts/bench-suite.sh`, `scripts/bench-report.py`) records CSVs under `scripts/bench-results/`.

## Knobs that actually move production

| Lever | Effect |

| Page-cache opt-in coverage and TTLs (app side) | The dominant lever: every hit removes a PHP render. |

| `--page-cache-admit-threshold 1` with dictionaries | Cache on first sight when storage is cheap; watch `httpjet_cache_hit_ratio_real`. |

| `--cf-send-zstd` | Hands the CDN the cheapest encoding to produce; no browser-visible change. |

| Fast-memo eligibility of the docroot chain | An ineligible chain (see `httpjet check`) pays the full pipeline on every static request; fix the directive rather than disabling the memo. |

| `--rewrite-ua-classify` | Collapses UA diversity on UA-reading chains onto a handful of outcome-cache entries. |

| TLS resumption & certified idle window | Full handshakes dominate behind a CDN that does not re-offer tickets; ECDSA chains, the single AES-128-GCM suite, `--tls-session-tickets 0` and `--trusted-proxy-idle-secs` keep handshake CPU low. |

| PHP: opcache, worker count, slow endpoints | Use `--php-slow-log` attribution; the pool is rarely the bottleneck (acquire p99.9

PAGE: Conformance & testing (https://httpjet.net/docs/conformance)
SUMMARY: h2spec 146/146, RFC coverage, LiteSpeed parity, the test layers, CI interoperability jobs, fuzzing, and the deploy gates.

# Conformance & testing

Two axes define httpjet's posture: **LiteSpeed compatibility** on the same configuration tree (LSWS 6.3.5 target — XML model, LSAPI, ETags, LSCache protocol, `.htaccess`), and **standards conformance** on the wire. Where they agree there is one right answer; where LiteSpeed made a deliberate choice a strict reading would call optional, httpjet matches LiteSpeed. Everything is held in place by ~3,000 tests, h2spec, fuzzing, CI interoperability jobs and the production deploy gates.

## Conformance matrix

| Area | Standard / reference | Status |

| HTTP/1.1 | RFC 9110 · RFC 9111 · RFC 9112 | Strict framing, conditional requests, single + multipart ranges (RFC 9110 §14), `Vary`, 103 Early Hints (RFC 8297); RFC 9112 request-target forms enforced at intake (origin-form; `*` OPTIONS-only; absolute-form reduced with its authority replacing Host), 405 for CONNECT, 400 for authority-form/raw `#`/bare-LF lines, Host required on HTTP/1.1 and validated by the h2 authority rule |

| HTTP/2 | RFC 9113 (native `hj-h2`) | **146 / 146** h2spec 2.6.0 over TLS; h2c informative 145/146 (documented dual-protocol exception) |

| HPACK | RFC 7541 | Zero-allocation codec; two fuzz targets |

| HTTP/3 / QUIC | RFC 9114 over RFC 9000 (quinn-proto), QPACK RFC 9204 | aioquic transfer and OTel trace fixtures in CI; migration disabled |

| TLS | rustls + aws-lc-rs · RFC 8446 mandatory suite | SNI mirrors OpenLiteSpeed; mTLS with CRLs; single-use tickets, 0-RTT off |

| ACME | RFC 8555 §8.1 / §8.3 (Pebble v2.10.1 fixtures) | HTTP-01 and DNS-01 behind `--features acme` |

| OCSP | RFC 6960 with the lightweight-profile conventions (SHA-256 issuer identity, bounded fetch — not full client conformance) | Behind `--features ocsp` |

| PROXY protocol | v2 binary + v1 text | Per-listener, fail-closed, pre-TLS/pre-sniff; loopback claims refused |

| LSAPI | Native wire codec (vendored php-src `lsapidef.h`) | Parity with `lsphp`; fuzzed response-header parser |

| FastCGI | FastCGI 1.0 (65,535-byte records, application record types) | Synthetic responder interoperability |

| ETag | LiteSpeed `fileETag=28` | `" - - ;;;"`, byte-for-byte |

| `.htaccess` | Apache mod_rewrite / mod_access / mod_auth_basic / mod_headers / mod_expires subset | Directive and flag parity for the common core (including `Expires*`, `Header merge` and APR1/MD5-crypt htpasswd); `Header` boundary characterized by fixtures |

| OpenTelemetry | OTLP HTTP/protobuf, W3C traceparent (version 00) | Behind `--features otel`; decoded-protobuf tests |

| LiteSpeed parity | Retired differential matrix vs LSWS 6.3.5 | 11 / 11 on the retained behaviors; now exercised continuously by production |

## LiteSpeed parity and the clean-room boundary

Differential testing against a live LiteSpeed reached 11/11 on ETag format, `.html`→PHP dispatch, LSAPI encoding and rewrite-flag semantics before the apparatus was retired: httpjet *is* now the same-config drop-in serving the live tree. The authoritative reference for LiteSpeed's exact behavior was the GPL OpenLiteSpeed source, read to extract *behavior* and then reimplemented from scratch — no OpenLiteSpeed code was copied. httpjet itself is licensed **GPL-3.0-only**, with no paid edition or license key, and is independent of and not endorsed by LiteSpeed Technologies.

           **fileETag=28** · byte-for-byte
```
ETag: "4096-1718800000-1572934;;;"     # size-mtime-inode, three trailing semicolons — strict validators compare bytes
```

Suffix routing and the `.html`→PHP decision follow OpenLiteSpeed's order, including the source-disclosure guard: a script whose handler has no pool is a 503 and never falls through to static.

## Test layers

| Layer | What it covers | Run |

| unit | Pure logic per crate: config parsing, rewrite evaluation, HPACK, ETags, cache keys, ACME snapshots, OCSP profiles, FastCGI records. | `cargo test -p ` |

| integration | Crate boundaries: real `.htaccess` files through the engine (`redirect_repro`, `header_compat`), upstream groups on ephemeral ports, page-cache expiry/race tests, full-pipeline e2e and security regressions in the binary, the H1 corpus replay (2,333 seed/truncation/mutation cases). | `cargo test --workspace` |

| live (`#[ignore]`) | Spawn `lsphp`, read real certificates, bind ports, QUIC round-trips, Pebble issuance. Run individually with their prerequisites; never as one batch. | `cargo test -- --ignored ` |

| scripts | Real-server fixtures on isolated loopback listeners: h2spec, ACME/OCSP/admin runtime tests, the cache gates, memo parity, OCI smoke. | see each page |

The last full runs: the whole workspace suite green at the 0.1.5 release (3,019 passed / 0 failed); 2,028 at 0.0.5. A failure is a regression, not "pre-existing." Timing-flaky meta-assertions were deleted in June 2026 so the concurrency tests are deterministic.

> [Diagram: verification-pyramid] Four-layer verification stack. Every change passes ~3,019 unit and integration tests, bounded corpus and ASan fuzz targets, protocol interoperability suites (h2spec 146/146, aioquic, Pebble ACME, OTel), and live loopback deploy gates before cutover.

## CI and interoperability jobs

- **Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64**: formatting, default and profiling builds, strict example-config validation, dependency-license and DCO checks, workspace tests, H1 corpus replay.

- **Ubuntu 22.04 x86_64 and Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64**: compile all features, replay H1, run the real io_uring UDS H1/H2 test — selected compatibility probes on GitHub-hosted runners, not a full kernel matrix.

- **Protocol interoperability**: an OTel-enabled binary, h2spec 2.6.0 over TLS against a fresh example configuration (archive SHA-256 pinned, exactly 146/146 required), H1 WebSocket / H2 dispatch tracing, and the aioquic 1.3.0 QUIC test in an isolated venv.

- **Dependency advisories**: a daily job fails on any RustSec finding and on a newer compatible transport-critical crate (quinn, rustls, aws-lc-rs, tokio, httparse, io-uring, zstd, brotli, h2, hyper, http, mio, socket2, openssl, bcrypt, libc).

- **Nightly/manual fuzz**: all eight parser targets with bounded time, input size, memory and artifact retention.

           **local reproduction**
```
cargo test --locked -p httpjet --test h1_corpus -- --nocapture
cargo build --locked -p httpjet --features otel --bin httpjet
python3 -B scripts/ci-h2spec.py --binary target/debug/httpjet --h2spec h2spec
cargo test --locked -p httpjet --features otel traced_fast_and_bridged_requests
cargo test --locked -p httpjet --features otel traced_quic_roundtrip -- --ignored
```

Hosted execution evidence is tracked separately from local runs; a runner label being available is not proof a job executed.

## Fuzzing

Eight `cargo-fuzz` targets share one invariant (never panic, never allocate unboundedly, agree with the reference decoder where one exists): `h1_chunked_decode`, `h1_request_framing`, `hpack_decode`, `hpack_roundtrip`, `lsapi_resp_header`, and — added in the 2026-10-06 review — `qpack_decode`, `proxy_protocol_parse` and `lscache_control`. Short ASan smoke runs of the original five covered 164,558 chunked, 739,373 framing, 452,899 HPACK-decode, 58,082 HPACK-roundtrip and 438,582 LSAPI-header executions without a finding.

           **bounded fuzz**
```
FUZZ_TOOLCHAIN=nightly FUZZ_SECONDS=5 bash scripts/fuzz-bounded.sh h1_request_framing
python3 scripts/fuzz-seeds.py     # regenerate the shared seed corpus
```

## Production gates

Beyond the suites, a deploy runs the cache-correctness gates (cross-URL, cross-scheme, cross-host, private tier, persistence), the fast-memo parity gate, the capsule purge gate and the h2spec gate. They are described with their failure classes on Page cache → deploy gates and Operations → deploy .

==============================================================================
PAGE: Migrating from LiteSpeed (https://httpjet.net/docs/migration)
SUMMARY: A validation-first migration path from LiteSpeed or OpenLiteSpeed: inventory, check --strict, isolated candidate, behavioral proof, caching, cutover and rollback.
==============================================================================

# Migrating from LiteSpeed

httpjet consumes LiteSpeed-compatible XML and LSAPI, but a migration is a **compatibility project**, not a binary swap that can skip validation. Directive coverage, filesystem identity, listener ownership, PHP supervision, TLS trust and cache behavior must each be proved for the target deployment. This is the path that proves them in order.

> [Diagram: migration-path] Eight steps, three gates. Nothing binds the incumbent ports until behavior — not just startup — has been proved on an isolated candidate; caching is introduced only after uncached parity.

## 1 · Inventory before changing traffic

- Main and per-vhost XML, included files, variables, listener/vhost maps.

- Document roots, symlink policy, `.htaccess` files, error documents, MIME maps, htpasswd files.

- TLS identities, chains, client-CA/CRL policy, renewal ownership (certbot? built-in ACME?), SNI maps.

- LSAPI processors, PHP environment, child limits, socket owner/mode, application health checks.

- Proxy/WebSocket targets, timeout and retry assumptions, trusted-proxy networks.

- Cache opt-in and purge headers, public/private variation, stale behavior, every external cache/CDN layer.

- Service user/group, writable paths, open-file/memory limits, socket activation, firewall rules, monitoring probes.

Keep secrets and host-specific paths out of migration reports and example repositories.

## 2 · Validate a copied configuration

           **gate 1**
```
target/release/httpjet --root /abs/copied-root check --strict
sudo -u   target/release/httpjet --root /abs/copied-root check --strict
```

Treat errors as blockers. Review every warning — ignored security elements (`lsrecaptcha`, `censorshipControl`), generic CGI contexts, wildcard maps, TLS over a Unix socket, unsupported auth forms, missing GeoIP data, unloaded vhosts, and settings that require a restart rather than a reload. *Parsed does not mean equivalent.* Compare the resulting listener/vhost map and effective limits with the source server, and run the check as the runtime identity too: readable-by-root is not proof the service user can read certificates or write logs, sockets and cache.

        !   Things LiteSpeed does that httpjet will not
`RequestHeader` and `Header edit` are ignored; traditional DES and `$5$`/`$6$` `crypt()` htpasswd hashes verify false (bcrypt, APR1 `$apr1$`, MD5-crypt `$1$` and `{SHA}` are supported); `Require` forms other than `all granted`/`valid-user`/`user` deny; anti-abuse elements are inert; `cacheStorePath` is unused; `respBuffer` always streams; `instances>1` is a single upstream. Each is on the capability matrix . You can also paste any `.htaccess` file into the interactive `.htaccess` & `fast_memo` readiness inspector to preview directive support and `MemoClass` eligibility in the browser.

## 3 · Build the smallest required binary

           **build**
```
CARGO_INCREMENTAL=0 cargo build --locked --release -p httpjet
```

Add `acme`, `ocsp`, `otel`, `profiling` or `ktls` only for a reviewed need, and keep every default-off feature and runtime switch off during initial parity testing. A `ktls` build defaults to `--ktls=auto`, which stays on rustls unless a physical NIC advertises active `tls-hw-tx-offload`.

## 4 · Start an isolated candidate

           **serve** · alternate everything
```
target/release/httpjet --root /abs/copied-root serve \
  --http-addr 127.0.0.1:18080 --https-addr 127.0.0.1:18443 --workers 1 \
  --php-socket /tmp/httpjet-migration-test.sock --php-children 4 \
  --metrics-addr 127.0.0.1:19090
```

Never bind the incumbent ports for the first run. Use loopback/alternate ports, a separate LSAPI socket (or an explicitly selected external test pool), distinct logs and a separate cache path. If PHP is out of scope use `--no-php` — and do not read that static fallback as PHP parity. Never point two supervisors at one LSAPI socket or process family.

## 5 · Prove behavior, not only startup

#### Routing & transport

- exact / default / foreign Host routing, HTTP→HTTPS behavior
- SNI, chain validation, ALPN, client certificates, CRL rejection
- h1 keep-alive and chunking, h2 multiplexing, h3 over UDP, large files, ranges, conditional requests, compression, HEAD

#### Application

- rewrite/redirect loops, front controllers, PATH_INFO, per-directory access, Basic auth, custom headers, error documents
- PHP/FastCGI environment, uploads, streaming, timeouts, worker recycling, source-disclosure failure cases
- proxy/WebSocket/SSE, upstream TLS identity, load distribution, all-backends-down, active-health recovery
- logs, request ids, metrics, readiness, graceful shutdown, restart, reload

Compare status, headers and body bytes with the incumbent where compatibility is required. Normalize inherently variable fields (Date, generated request ids) explicitly — do not discard all headers to make a comparison pass.

## 6 · Introduce caching separately

Leave `--page-cache` off until uncached parity is established. Then, with an isolated cache and conservative caps, prove that distinct paths, hosts, schemes, queries, cookies, sessions and encodings cannot replay one another; public responses never store private cookies or authenticated data; private entries are session-bound; purge tags invalidate every tier; stale-if-error and stale-while-revalidate obey their windows; restart scanning, integrity failures, missing files and capacity eviction are fail-safe; and the upstream CDN does not retain redirects or errors longer than intended. The repository's cache gates are the executable form of this list. A cache that looks fast but is keyed wrongly is a data-isolation defect, not a performance win.

## 7 · Stage traffic and retain rollback

Package the exact tested binary at a stable path. Prefer a service manager that can hold listener ownership (socket activation), apply non-root permissions, set limits and restart on failure — validate the systemd or OCI example against your environment rather than copying it. Canary through an existing load balancer or CDN, or a dedicated address, before a full listener handoff. Monitor status classes, backend latency and errors, cache dispositions, active connections, memory, file descriptors, PHP/upstream health and h1/h2/h3 traffic independently.

Write and *drill* the rollback before cutover: the prior binary, configuration, unit, certificate ownership, application socket and cache/CDN purge procedure. A binary rollback does not remove bad objects already stored in origin or edge caches.

## 8 · Reload only what is reloadable

Validate before SIGHUP or an API submission. Application-compatible state publishes while existing requests finish on the old generation; listener/QUIC/Unix-socket topology, PHP topology, cache-store identity, process privileges and other boot-owned resources need a restart. An API `restart_required` result is a safety boundary, not a suggestion to force the transaction. See Admin API & reload .

## Minimum acceptance record

- Source commit and build features.

- Sanitized configuration fingerprint (`vhost-map-fingerprint`) and validation output.

- Service identity, kernel/runtime, resource limits.

- Exact test commands, protocol clients, pass/fail counts.

- Canary window and the observed error/cache/backend deltas.

- The rollback command and a successful rollback drill.

Do not claim completion from source inspection, a successful compile or one HTTP 200. The migration is complete when the intended workload, failure modes, operations and rollback have been exercised in the target environment.
